The primary objective of this paper is to lay down the theoretical foundations of a MPC framework for hybrid dynamical system, with the meaning of “hybrid” as clarified above. In contrast to the aforementioned works, the present approach directly incorporates hybrid time domains and trajectory evolution into the prediction and constraint structure, allowing for general, continuous-time hybrid dynamics beyond piecewise-affine, impulsive, or switched-only systems. Although modern MPC developments, such as economic and dissipativity-based MPC, turnpike phenomena, and formulations without terminal ingredients, offer powerful alternatives in continuous settings, their extension to hybrid systems is nontrivial and remains an open research direction. This paper focuses on transferring and formalizing early MPC principles in the hybrid context, providing a foundation for future integration of these newer techniques.

B. Contributions

Although the concept of applying MPC to hybrid systems has existed in literature for several decades, an MPC framework for hybrid plants of the form (1) is not yet available. This paper provides a comprehensive presentation of hybrid MPC for such systems, and formally introduces the structural conditions and theoretical tools needed to ensure:

1) Appropriate structure and properties of the hybrid prediction horizon;
2) Forward invariance of the terminal constraint set and of the feasible set (Proposition 5.1 and Proposition 5.2);
3) That the value function serves as a Lyapunov function via bounds in terms of the terminal and stage costs (Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.5);
4) Positive definiteness of the value function (multiple results in Section V-D and Section V-E);
5) Asymptotic stability of a closed set via hybrid MPC, including special cases when jumps or flows are persistent (Theorem 6.2);
6) Two examples showing in detail how to apply the results.

The results are illustrated in two examples throughout the paper, one pertaining to control of a bouncing ball and another one about sample-and-hold control. The overall framework was first outlined in the conference paper [29], which informally presents an initial version of the framework presented here but does not include any mathematical result. The conference paper [30] presents a preliminary version of the basic assumptions. These assumptions are relaxed here; in particular, the set to asymptotically stabilize does no longer need to be compact, expanding the applicability of our results to a broader class of stabilization problems (e.g., consensus, tracking, and estimation), and a condition relating the terminal constraint set and the set to asymptotically stabilize is removed (see (O4) in [30]). A result revealing properties of the value function was stated without proof in [30, Lemma 5.4 and Lemma 5.5], but significantly improved here, under weaker assumptions (cf. Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.5) and allowing the stage costs and the terminal cost to be not be positive definite. The latter results can be found in Section V-D and Section V-E, which further extend the relaxations in the conference paper [31] – in fact, only a version of items 2 and 3 in Theorem 5.6 are considered therein, which are further relaxed in those sections. Note that [30] and [31] do not include i) any mathematical proofs, ii) the intermediate results required to establish the properties of the value function and asymptotic stability, and iii) the many illustrations via examples, given by two examples revisited throughout the paper multiple times.

C. Organization of the Paper

Section II introduces notation and basic concepts of hybrid systems. Section III presents an overview of hybrid MPC and its main ingredients: the cost functional, the prediction horizon, the constrained optimal control problem, and the recursive implementation of hybrid MPC. The assumptions required for hybrid MPC to be asymptotically stabilizing are presented in Section IV. Section V reveals the main properties of the constrained optimal control problem associated with hybrid MPC. Section V-D characterizes properties guaranteeing positive definiteness of the value function. Section VI formalizes the asymptotic stabilization properties of hybrid MPC. Section VII presents examples to which the main results are applied. Open problems and future work are discussed in Section VIII.

II. Background on Hybrid Control Systems

Throughout the paper, we use \(\mathbb{R}\) to represent real numbers and \(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) its nonnegative subset. The set of nonnegative integers is denoted \(\mathbb{N}\). The notation \(S_{1} \subset S_{2}\) indicates \(S_{1}\) is a subset of \(S_{2}\), not necessarily proper. The 2-norm is denoted \(|\cdot|\). The distance of a vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) to a nonempty set \(\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\) is denoted \(|\textbf{x}|_{\mathcal{A}} \coloneqq \inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} |\textbf{x} - a|\). We denote by \(\mathcal{A} + \delta\mathbb{B}\) the set of all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\) such that \(|\textbf{x} - a| \leq \delta\) for some \(a \in \mathcal{A}\). The interior and closure of a set \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\) are denoted int \(S\) and cl \(S\), respectively. We denote by \(\Pi : \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}^{n}\) the standard projection onto \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\) such that \(\Pi(x, y) = x\). A strictly increasing continuous function \(\alpha : \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) with \(\alpha(0) = 0\) is said to be a class-\(\mathcal{K}\) function. An unbounded class-\(\mathcal{K}\) function is said to be a class-\(\mathcal{K}_{\infty}\) function.

* •the flow set \(C \subset \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \mathbb{R}^{m}\);
* •the flow map \(f : C \to \mathbb{R}^{n}\) describes the continuous evolution of \(x\) when \((x, u)\) belongs to \(C\);

The next result can be obtained using similar steps as in the proof of [18, Proposition 2.11].

**Proposition 2.8:** The hybrid control system \(\mathcal{H}\) has unique state trajectories if and only if Assumption 2.7 holds.

**Proof:** Necessity is obvious. For sufficiency, consider two solution pairs \((x,u)\) and \((x^{\prime},u^{\prime})\) with the same initial condition and domain, where \(u\) and \(u^{\prime}\) are equivalent. Since jumps of \(x\) and \(x^{\prime}\) occur at the same ordinary time, uniqueness follows from uniqueness during flows (by Assumption 2.7) and uniqueness during jumps.

**Remark 2.9:** For hybrid dynamical systems with single-valued flow and jump maps and no inputs (i.e., closed hybrid systems), uniqueness of solutions is guaranteed when flows are not possible on the intersection of the flow and jump sets, and the constrained differential equation (8) has unique solutions [18, Proposition 2.11] and [19, Proposition 2.34]. In contrast, Assumption 2.7 states that uniqueness during flows is necessary and sufficient for uniqueness of state trajectories. This property is due to the fact that given any two solution pairs \((x,u)\) and \((x^{\prime},u)\), their jump times are determined by the domain of the input; hence, by Definition 2.3, \(\operatorname{dom}(x,u)=\operatorname{dom}(x^{\prime},u)=\operatorname{dom}u\).

**III. Hybrid MPC: Key Elements and Algorithm**

In this section, we introduce the main elements required to formulate an MPC algorithm to asymptotically stabilize the hybrid plant \(\mathcal{H}\) in (1).

**A. Overview**

In simple words, the algorithm measures the current state of \(\mathcal{H}\) and finds an optimal solution pair to \(\mathcal{H}\) over a finite horizon in hybrid time. The optimization problem consists of minimizing a cost functional, subject to constraints on the terminal time and terminal state. The cost functional assesses the cost of the evolution of the state and of the possible inputs to be applied, both over intervals of flows and at time instances at which jumps occur. The cost functional imposes a cost on the terminal state, relative to a desired target set. This optimization is performed over a hybrid prediction horizon, and the terminal hybrid time is allowed to vary within a set rather than being restricted to a point, as done, for instance, in discrete-time MPC where the optimization involves a fixed prediction horizon. This optimization approach is reminiscent of free end-time optimal control. It is instrumental for MPC for hybrid systems as the hybrid time domain of an optimal solution pair is not known a priori. Each time the state is measured, the algorithm finds an optimal control hybrid input that is applied to \(\mathcal{H}\) until the next measurement, leading to a receding horizon implementation. The initial optimization occurs at the initial time \((t,j)=(0,0)\). We refer to this algorithm as hybrid MPC.

There are three main differences between conventional continuous-time/discrete-time MPC, in their general formulations, and hybrid MPC:

* Since hybrid control systems can have solution pairs from nearby initial conditions with drastically different hybrid time domains, the terminal time has to be allowed to vary within a set. This set is the hybrid prediction horizon introduced above.

* To account for the differences in the hybrid time domains of optimal control hybrid inputs, the optimization times are not assumed to be periodic or known a priori. Instead, with the initial optimization being performed at time \((0,0)\), each subsequent optimization hybrid time is selected online and the reoptimization occurs before the current hybrid control input is exhausted.

* Since hybrid plants typically involve timer states, logic variables, and memory states, as Example 2.6 illustrates, the problem that hybrid MPC has to solve may be a set stabilization problem rather than a set-point stabilization problem. In fact, the stabilization problem associated with Example 2.6 consists of asymptotic stabilizing the state \(z\) to zero, \(\eta\) to some compact set, and \(\tau_{s}\) to the range \([0,T_{s}]\).

Remark 3.8 (About Discretization): Problem 3.5 is formulated for the hybrid plant $\mathcal{H}$ in (1). Note that the flows of $\mathcal{H}$ are not explicitly discretized in the implementation given in Algorithm 1. Such a discretization can be made explicit by choosing a discretization method for $\hat{x} = f(x, u)$ and defining solutions to the resulting system on discretized hybrid time domains—indeed, they are defined over hybrid time domains. Discretization for hybrid systems for the purposed of hybrid MPC are presented in [34], along with a method to solve Problem 3.5 with discretized flows; see also [35].  

Remark 3.9 (Computing a Solution to Problem 3.5): Computation of an optimal solution to Problem 3.5 is a nontrivial task. In certain cases, Problem 3.5 can be solved by converting it into a finite- dimensional nonlinear program. The development of general numerical methods to solve Problem 3.5 is the current object of research, and can take the form of the maximum principle—see [36] and the references therein. The approaches in [34] and [35] solve Problem 3.5 with discretized flows. They algorithms therein use adaptations of off- the- shelf optimization solvers for mixed- integer nonlinear programs, with potentially large computational times. Note that [37] provide conditions under which the optimal cost can be continuously approximated numerically.  

## IV. Main Assumptions  

We list the basic assumptions imposed on Problem 3.5 to ensure feasibility and certify asymptotic stability of a given closed set $\mathcal{A} \subset X$ of interest. The required assumptions resemble those typically assumed in continuous-time and discrete-time MPC, when generalized to the set stabilization problem.6 Combined with the hybrid prediction horizon defined in Definition 3.2, the forthcoming assumptions guarantee most of the properties required to establish asymptotic stability, with the exception of positive definiteness of the value function, which is studied in depth in the forthcoming Sections V- D and V- E, as it can be achieved in multiple ways.  

The following assumptions assert basic positive definiteness properties and bounds on the cost functions. These properties are used in establishing positive definiteness of the value function and asymptotic stability of the closed- loop system resulting from using hybrid MPC.  

Assumption 4.1: Given a hybrid plant $\mathcal{H} = (C, f, D, g)$, a closed set $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, flow cost $L_C$, and jump cost $L_D$,  

( W1) There exists a class- $K_{\infty}$ function $\alpha_C$ such that $L_C(x, u) \geq \alpha_C(|x|_\mathcal{A})$ for each $(x, u) \in C$ ( W2) There exists a class- $K_{\infty}$ function $\alpha_D$ such that $L_D(x, u) \geq \alpha_D(|x|\mathcal{A})$ for each $(x, u) \in D$  

Assumption 4.2: Given a closed set $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, a terminal constraint set $X$, and a terminal cost function $V$, there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ and a class- $K$ function $\alpha$ such that $V(x) \leq \alpha(|x|_{\mathcal{A}})$ for each $x \in X \cap (\mathcal{A} + \varepsilon \mathbb{B})$  

The key stabilizing ingredient of our hybrid MPC algorithm is given by the following familiar CLF- like assumption requiring the existence of a (static) state- feedback pair $\kappa=(\kappa_C,\kappa_D)$. Below,forward pre- invariance of $X$ means that every maximal closed- loop solution with initial state in $X$ is complete and stays in $X$ [38, Definition 3.1], and forward completeness of $X$ means that for every point $X$ there exists a complete solution. A weaker notion of invariance is weak forward invariance, which is used in the next section and simply requires that from each point in $X$, there exists a maximal and complete solution that stays in $X$.  

Assumption 4.3: Given a hybrid plant $\mathcal{H} = (C, f, D, g)$, a closed set $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, flow cost $L_C$, jump cost $L_D$, terminal constraint set $X$, and terminal cost $V$, there exists a state- feedback law $\kappa = (\kappa_C,\kappa_D)$ such that the terminal constraint set $X$ is forward pre- invariant and forward complete for the hybrid system $\mathcal{H}$ in (9). Moreover, the terminal cost $V$ is differentiable on an open set containing. $\mathrm{cl}(X \cap C_\kappa)$, and

Proof. Given the optimal solution \((x, u)\), we recall the feasible solution pair derived in the proof of Lemma 5.2 that starts from \(x(t,j)\). Call this solution pair \((z, v)\), and note that after time \((T - t, J - j) \in \text{dom}(z, v)\), \((z, v)\) corresponds to a solution generated by the feedback \(\kappa\), say \((x', u')\), where \((T, J)\) is the terminal time of \((x, u)\). Then, observe that \(\mathcal{I}^*(x(t,j)) \le \mathcal{I}(z, v)\) as \((z, v)\) is not \(\mathcal{I}^*(x(t, j)) \le \mathcal{I}(z, v)\) as \((z, v)\) is not optimal. The following holds:
\[
\mathcal{I}^*(x(t,j)) \le \mathcal{I}(z, v) = \mathcal{I}(z, u) \\
= \sum_{i=0}^{j} \int_{s_i}^{s_{i+1}} L_C(x(s,i), u(s,i)) ds \\
- \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} L_D(x(s_{i+1}, i), u(s_{i+1}, i)) \\
- V(x(T, j)) + \mathcal{I}(x', u')
\]
The bound \(\mathcal{I}(z, v)\) follows from the fact that \((z, v)\) starts from \(x(t,j)\) and that \((z, v)\) is not optimal. The equality captures the following fact: the cost of \((x, u)\), which is up to \((T, J)\), plus the cost of \((x', u')\) is equal to the cost of \((x, u)\) up to \((t, j)\) plus the cost of \((z, v\)). By solving for the cost of \((z, v)\) from this relationship we obtain the equality above. Finally, since \(x(t, j) = x'(0, 0)\), the term \(- V(x(t, j)) + \mathcal{I}(x', u') \) is nonpositive by Lemma 5.3, leading to the desired result as \(\mathcal{I}(x, u) = \mathcal{I}^*(x(0, 0))\) since \((x, u)\) is optimal.

\[
|x(s,i)|_{\mathcal{A}} \ge \alpha(|x(0, 0)|_{\mathcal{A}})
\]
4. for all \((s, i) \in \text{dom}(x, u)\) satisfying \(t + j \le s + i \le t' + j'\);

7. there exist an open neighborhood \(\mathcal{U}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) and a continuous function \(\sigma : \mathbb{R} \ge 0 \to \mathbb{R} \ge 0\) such that

Remark 5.7: The solution-dependent conditions in Theorem 5.6 guarantees required properties to guarantee positive definiteness of the value function. Conditions P1)-P4) therein relax positive definiteness properties of the stage costs and terminal cost, in particular, to allow for the stage cost for flows or jumps to be zero, which permits the user to not associate a cost to flows or jumps, respectively. For instance, for solution pairs with persistent jumps, item 3 relaxes positive definiteness of the flow cost \( L_C \) and terminal cost \( V \) by assuming a property on optimal solution pairs \((x, u) \) originating away from \(\cal A\) - see condition P3). This property guarantees that \(x \) is away from \(\cal A \) at a jump time, which ensures that the cost of \((x, u) \) is nonzero. A similar relaxation is possible for the jump cost \( L_D \), via item 2, through the use of P2). Note that the conditions in item 2 relax those in item 1 by requiring the flow cost to be positive definite when flows are persistent, as captured by P2). A similar comment applies to item 3. Item 7 exploits condition P5) to establish the lower bound, similar to results in the standard MPC literature, at the price of requiring positive definiteness of \( L_C, L_D \), and \( V \). Note that P5) implies the existence of a uniform upper bound on the magnitude of the velocity of the state trajectories from nearby \(\cal A \), and that is satisfied when \(f \) is continuous, \(\cal A \) is compact, and \( C = C' \times U \) for some closed set \( C' \subset \mathbb{R}^n \) and some compact set \( U \subset \mathbb{R}^m \), which corresponds to the typical assumptions on state and input constraints in the MPC literature.

III) it terminates at time \((T, 0)\) with \(T \leq \alpha'(|x(0, 0)|_A)\) and, hence, satisfies P4) with \(J = 0\), both with \(\alpha = \alpha'\).

In the case of the time horizon \(\mathcal{T}\) being bounded away from the origin considered in item a).i), P1) holds with \(\alpha = \alpha'\) since each feasible solution pair \((x, u)\) is such that there exists \((t', j') \in \text{dom}(x, u)\) such that \(t' + j' \geq c > 0\), which, in turn, implies that there exists \((t, j) \in \text{dom}(x, u)\) such that \(t + j \leq t' + j'\) and \(t' - t + j - j' \geq \alpha'(|x(0, 0)|_A)\).

Finally, P2) or P4) hold under the conditions in b). Without loss of generality, suppose that \(\sigma\) in (25) is such that there exists \(c > 0\) such that \(\sigma(r) \geq c\) for all \(r > 0\). With \(\varepsilon\) coming from (25), let

\[\varphi(r) := \max_{r' \in [r/2, r]} \sigma(r') \quad \forall \varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon] \tag{27}\]

which satisfies \(\varphi(r) \geq c\) for all \(r \in (0, \varepsilon]\). Continuity of \(\varphi\) follows via Berge’s maximum theorem [41, Theorem 1.4.16] by showing upper and lower semicontinuity of the set-valued map mapping each \(r \in [0, \varepsilon]\) to the compact interval \([r/2, r]\). Indeed, lower semicontinuity of the mapping can be verified directly, while upper semicontinuity follows from the fact that the mapping is outer semicontinuous (since its graph is closed relative to \((0, \varepsilon] \times \mathbb{R}\) [18, Lemma 5.10]) and locally bounded, due to [18, Lemma 5.15]. Let \(\tau(0) := 0\) and

\[\tau(r) := \begin{cases} x/r, & \text{if } r \in (0, \varepsilon] \\ r/t_1, & \text{if } r \in (\varepsilon, \infty) \end{cases}\]

and similarly, for every \(r \geq 0\), let \(\rho(r) := \min\{r, \varepsilon\}\). Note that \(\tau\) is continuous, positive definite, upper bounded by \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\varphi(\varepsilon)}\), and lower bounded by zero. Hence, there exists a continuous function \(\tilde{\tau} : \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) that is positive definite, increasing, and such that \(\tilde{\tau}(r) \leq \tau(r)\) for all \(r \geq 0\). It follows that, for any continuous solution pair \((x, u)\) to \(\mathcal{H}\) with \(|x(0, 0)|_A > 0\), \(t < \tilde{\tau}(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A))\) satisfying \((t, 0) \in \text{dom}(x, u)\) implies \(|x(t, 0)|_A \geq \frac{\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A)}{2}\). To show this implication, first note that, by definition of \(\tilde{\tau}\), \(\tilde{\tau}(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A))\) is upper bounded by \(\tau(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A))\) and that, since \(\rho\) is upper bounded by \(\varepsilon\), \(\tilde{\tau}(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A)) \varphi(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A)) \leq \frac{\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A)}{\varepsilon}\). Then, the lower bound on \(|x(t, 0)|_A\) can be obtained by evaluating the latter inequality at \(t = \tilde{\tau}(\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A))\), leading to \(|x(t, 0)|_A \geq \frac{\rho(|x(0, 0)|_A)}{2}\). In other words, \(\tilde{\tau} \circ \rho(r)\) is a lower bound on the ordinary time to reach the \((r/2)\)-disc around \(\mathcal{A}\) from the \(r\)-disc around \(\mathcal{A}\) via flows, for each \(r \geq 0\). Finally, for every \(r \geq 0\), let \(\hat{\alpha}_D(r) := \hat{\alpha}_D(\rho(r)/2)\), and note that \(\hat{\alpha}_D\) and \(\rho\) are continuous, nondecreasing, and positive definite.

Let \((x, u)\) be an optimal solution pair and \(\{t_j\}_{j=0}^{J+1}\) be a sequence such that \(\text{dom}(x, u) = \bigcup_{j=0}^{J} ([t_j, t_{j+1}] \times \{j\})\), with \(|x(0, 0)|_A > 0\). While not emphasized in Definition 6.1, note that in general, from any initial condition \(x_{\circ} \in \mathcal{X}\) , there might be infinitely many solution pairs generated by the hybrid MPC algorithm. SolutionThe solution of the given problem involves finding the roots of the function \(L_C(x, u) = \begin{bmatrix} a_{\text{hot}}(z - z_{\text{max}}) + a_{\text{on}}q & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\text{D}_{C}(x, u) = \begin{bmatrix} a_{\text{cold}}(z_{\text{min}} - z) & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{min}} \\ a_{\text{on}} & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \end{bmatrix}\). The function \(L_C(x, u)\) is defined as the sum of four functions, each of which has a specific range of values. A gradient descent algorithm is used to find the roots and the coefficients of the functions. The algorithm is as follows:

1. \(a_{\text{hot}}(z - z_{\text{max}}) + a_{\text{on}}q \leq 1\) for all \(z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}})\)

2. \(a_{\text{on}} \leq 1\) for all \(z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}})\)

3. \(a_{\text{cold}}(z_{\text{min}} - z) \leq 1\) for all \(z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}})\)

4. \(a_{\text{on}} \leq 1\) for all \(z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}})\)

The coefficients \(a_{\text{hot}}, a_{\text{on}}, a_{\text{cold}}, a_{\text{on}}\) are updated iteratively using the gradient descent algorithm.

The main control action \(V\) is given by

\[V(x) = \begin{cases} (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{min}})^2 & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{min}} \\ \text{D}_2(x, u) = \begin{bmatrix} (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{min}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{min}} \end{bmatrix} \end{cases}\]

The main control output is given by \(V(x)\) for all \(x\) in the region specified by the constraints \(\mathcal{U}\). The main control action \(V\) is given by

\[V(x) = \begin{cases} z \in \mathcal{U} & \text{if } z \notin \mathcal{X} \\ z = x + b & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \\ \text{D}_3(x, u) = -c_{\text{on}}(z - z_{\text{max}}) - c_{\text{on}} & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \\ \text{D}_4(x, u) = -c_{\text{on}} & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \end{cases}\]

where \(c_{\text{on}}\) is the coefficient of the cooling function and \(c_{\text{nond}}\) is its threshold. The main control output is given by

\[V(x) = -\text{c}_{\text{on}}(z - z_{\text{max}}) - \text{c}_{\text{on}}\]

The main control output is given by

\[V(x,u) = \begin{cases} (z - z_{\text{min}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \\ \text{D}_5(x, u) = \begin{bmatrix} (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{min}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{min}} \end{bmatrix} \end{cases}\]

The main control output is given by

\[V(x,u) = \begin{cases} (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \end{cases}\]

The main control output is given by

\[V(x,u) = \begin{cases} z \in \mathcal{U} & \text{if } z \notin \mathcal{X} \\ z = x + b & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \\ \text{D}_6(x, u) = \begin{cases} (z - z_{\text{max}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ (z - z_{\text{min}})^2 & \text{if } z > z_{\text{max}} \\ \text{D}_7(x, u) = -c_{\text{on}}(z - z_{\text{max}}) - c_{\text{on}} & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \\ \text{D}_8(x, u) = -c_{\text{on}} & \text{if } z \in \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{U} \end{cases}\]

where the terms \((1+q)\) and \((2-q)\) penalize being at the "wrong" mode. Picking the feedback \(\kappa_C\) as \(\kappa_C(x) = 0\) if \(x \in \widetilde{C}\), and one otherwise, and the feedback \(\kappa_D\) as \(\kappa_D(x) = 1\) if \(x \in \widetilde{D}\), and zero otherwise, we obtain the following properties for the variation of \(V\) along flows and jumps of the hybrid closed-loop system \(\mathcal{H}_{\kappa}\) in (9): for every \(x \in X \cap \widetilde{C} = \widetilde{C}\) we have that \(\langle \nabla V(x), f(x, \kappa_C(x)) \rangle\) is given by

\[\begin{cases} -(z_{\text{max}} - z_0)(z - z_{\text{max}}) & \text{if } z \geq z_{\text{max}} \\ 0 & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ -(z_0 + z_{\Delta} - z_{\text{min}})(z_{\text{min}} - z) & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{min}} \end{cases}\]

and, for every \(x \in X \cap \widetilde{D} = \widetilde{D}\), \(V(g(x, \kappa_D(x))) - V(x)\) is equal to

\[\begin{cases} -\frac{(z - z_{\text{max}})^2}{2} & \text{if } z \geq z_{\text{max}} \\ \frac{0}{2} & \text{if } z \in (z_{\text{min}}, z_{\text{max}}) \\ -\frac{(z - z_{\text{min}})^2}{2} & \text{if } z \leq z_{\text{min}} \end{cases}\]

It follows that, with the choices of \(L_C\) and \(L_D\) above, Assumption 4.3 holds and that \(X\) is forward pre-invariant for \(\mathcal{H}_{\kappa}\). From item P5) in Theorem 5.6, there exists a class-\(\mathcal{K}\) function \(\alpha^*: \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) such that the value function \(\mathcal{J}^*\) in (14) satisfies (19) for each \(x_o \in \mathcal{X}\). Finally, from [37, Section 6.1], we have that an optimal solution pair \((x, u) \in \widehat{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{H}}(x_o)\) exists from each such \(x_o\).

**VII. Conclusion**

This paper formalizes an MPC framework for hybrid dynamical systems. The formulation allows to quantify the cost and predict trajectories over hybrid time domains. Conditions guaranteeing recursive feasibility, positive definiteness of the value function and its decrease along solutions, leading to asymptotic stability of a closed set are proposed. The conditions involve the data of the system and the OCP, leading to checkable design conditions. Future work will focus on the hybrid MPC design to satisfy other dynamical properties of interest, such as safety, temporal logic, and robustness. An add-on to our Hybrid Equations Toolbox (HyEQ) for Matlab/Simulink [42] to compute numerical solutions of Problem 3.5 is currently being developed. Employing the results in [43] to relax the conditions for positive definiteness of the value function as suggested by an anonymous reviewer is also part of future work.
